One-Owner 1972 Camaro Hasn't Moved Since Last Millennium, Hides Biggest Small-Block Surprise
51 photos
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast
The second generation of the Camaro was a roller coaster of extreme proportions, recording both he lowest and the highest production volumes of the that iteration. In 1972, the moniker dropped to an abyssal 68k units, while in 1979 it managed to sell more than 214,000 MORE than in ’72. And this example, coming from that very ill-fated season, sat for almost three decades, patiently waiting for its owner who bought it new to put it back on the road. That wait is over.
1972 was not a good year to be a Camaro. Or a Chevrolet, in general. Or anything General Motors, quite frankly. United Auto Workers had had just about enough of GM’s attitude and walked out of their work stations at the Norwood facility. That was in April. They came back in September.
It doesn’t take a rocket science to see that the strike lasted almost half a year, with the direct consequence being production numbers suffered enormous setbacks. As such, scrupulous gearheads might say that the ‘72s are somewhat… rare ? Maybe not – 68,651 is still a fairly large volume (the Plymouth Barracuda, for example, never managed to hit that mark in its entire decade-long stint), but for the Bowtie pony car, it was a counter-performance of cataclysmic proportions.
So big, in fact, that the brass hats from corporate considered axing the moniker. They eventually ruled in favor of keeping it – thankfully, otherwise the car we see in the video embedded below might have been one of the last Chevrolet Camaros ever made. However, it’s probably among the very few that haven’t seen the light of the third millennium at all, having been shoved in a garage before we started writing the year with a “2” at the beginning.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast Picture this. You crack open a dusty garage door and find a 1972 Chevrolet Camaro that has not seen daylight since 1999. It sat there for 27 years just waiting for someone to drag it out. A guy started swapping the intake manifold on a 400 cubic-inch small block V8, got sidetracked, and walked away. The car basically became a shelf until the right wrenchers finally came along.
Those right guys run the Not So Fast YouTube channel. Nathan McInnis and his buddy rolled up with a trailer, strapped the Chevy down, and hauled it back to their shop. You would expect a complete rust bucket after almost three decades, but this Midwest survivor was put only on hold, not on the deathroll. The paint held up well, and engine internals were shockingly clean.
The wrenchers knew better than to just turn the key and pray for luck. They had a method – the right one. The correct approach. The way to do it properly. The true died-in-the-wool piston-head mentality. They started from ground zero, tore out the fuel system. They dropped in a brand-new tank, ran fresh rubber lines, and bolted up a replacement sending unit.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast The car’s fluids were drained – block, transmission, rear end, radiator, the pans dropped (engine and cogbox), the differential thoroughly inspected, and then the car received a fresh supply of lubricants and coolant.
Then they yanked the distributor out to manually prime the oil pump. Turning that crank by hand ensured the engine would not chew up its own bearings. Once they saw oil flowing properly, they dumped two-stroke fuel straight down the large carburetor throats.
The old V8 roared to life on the very first try. It smoked out the entire shop, but it ran. Dan yelled, "It is alive!" as the exhaust cleared. They chased down a nasty coolant leak blowing out of a loose thermostat housing. They also discovered a cross threaded brass oil pressure sending unit dumping fluid everywhere. Because old units use actual pressure to read gauges, they fixed it immediately.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast Brakes came next, because stopping is somewhat important when one plans to drive their old Camaro after a hefty 27-year pause. In fact, come to think of it, it’s important, no matter what car it may be. They tossed the rusted brake booster and bolted on a fresh master cylinder. They replaced wheel cylinders, ran new hoses, and slapped on some brake pads and rotors.
Throwing on a fresh set of tires, they took the resurrected Chevy around the neighborhood. It clicked through the automatic gears perfectly. "First drive in 27 years. It runs really great!" That pretty much sums it up. If only all classic car resurrections were this successful on the first try…
They took it out on the highway next, cruising smoothly at 60 mph. one of the mechanics rightfully noted no one would never know this thing had been sitting for so long. The boys were having fun with 400 cubes of old-school small-block torque from an age long before they were born. This car is not a factory performance package model, it was born a run-of-the-mill 350, as the fender badges proclaim.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast Someone decided a base Camaro deserved better, and threw the biggest-ever Chevy small-block at it (by displacement, not physical sizes). That makes this street brawler the perfect candidate for a budget backyard resurrection.
Seeing a 1972 Camaro back on the road stirs up the history a bit. Back in ‘72, you could walk into a dealership and pick between a few distinct flavors. You had the base model, the split bumper Rally Sport, the Super Sport, or the corner carving Z/28 performance package. The base model, just like our rescue car started out, was the volume leader. Most people bought the standard version because it looked great and did not completely empty out your bank account then.
Let us break down those production numbers . Out of that strike shortened run, buyers opted for 11,364 Rally Sport appearance packages. Another 6,562 customers stepped up to buy the Super Sport version. Only 2,575 buyers shelled out for the hardcore track version. That leaves the vast majority of cars built – 48,139 units – as standard base models. The base coupe started at a very reasonable 2,729 dollars with a six-cylinder engine.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast If you wanted V8 power, the base 8-cylinder model sticker price bumped up to 2,819 dollars. Engine options were solid across the entire lineup. The entry level motor was a 250 cubic-inch sixer pushing 110 horsepower. The base V8 was a 307-cuber with 130 horsepower. Next up was the signature 350 cubic-inch V8 (that had debuted hand in hand with the Camaro moniker itself, in the fall of ’66, as a 1967 model) that delivered 165 horsepower for the regular daily street cruiser buyer.
Those wanting even more grunt could grab the Super Sport, which offered a 402 cubic-inch big-block throwing down 240 horsepower, and hidden behind a “396” badge, for marketing purposes. The Z28 offered a high-revving 350 cubic-inch solid-lifter engine pushing 255 horsepower. All numbers are net ratings, because SAE said so.
Chevrolet gave buyers plenty of transmission choices to pair with these engines. You could grab a 3-speed manual, a 4-speed manual, or let the car do the shifting itself. If you wanted an automatic, you got the 2-speed Powerglide on lower models or the heavy-duty 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic. Imagine the audacity of carmakers from 50+ years ago when giving windshield wipers the same number of speeds as the car itself…
